title: LLM API Battlecard: Positioning Tactics & Reps Playbook
content:
Purpose
This is a lightweight, rep-focused battlecard and messaging playbook for positioning Redwood Inference vs other LLM API providers. Use this in discovery calls, deal reviews, and for prepping objection responses. Keep it conversational — the goal is to help reps quickly map customer pain to Redwood strengths.

Audience and usage
- Sales reps (AE/BDR) and solutions engineers preparing for 30–60 minute discovery calls.
- Marketing/SDRs for brief email/LinkedIn scripts.
- Product and GTM to capture gaps and update messaging.

Top customer archetypes to target in call prep
1) Platform teams standardizing AI across product lines (care about consistent API, observability, rollout controls).
2) Fast-growing startups prioritizing developer experience and cost predictability.
3) Regulated enterprises needing private deployments and compliance controls.
4) ML teams with bursty inference patterns who need predictable latency and capacity.

Primary positioning thesis (elevator):
"Redwood is the production-first inference platform that gives you predictable latency, transparent unit economics, and consistent operational controls whether you use hosted, dedicated, or private deployments — so engineering teams ship LLM features without building their own serving stack."

Competitor archetypes & what they lean on
- Hyperscaler LLM APIs (big cloud providers): wide reach, bundled infra, ecosystem integrations. Weakness: opaque per-token economics, limited fallback/rollout options, and sometimes model lock-in.
- Boutique LLM API vendors (small-scale providers): developer-friendly and fast to start. Weakness: less operational maturity, limited enterprise SLAs, and narrower model catalog.
- Open-source model platforms / self-hosted runtimes: great for control and cost at scale. Weakness: heavy ops burden and long time-to-production.

Feature comparison cheat-sheet (talking points)
- Latency SLOs: Redwood supports SLA-backed latency guarantees for Dedicated customers + regional routing to meet SLOs.
- Cost transparency: Token-level cost breakdowns and Optimize suggestions (batching, quantization) to reduce unit cost.
- Rollouts & fallbacks: Canary/A-B rollouts, automatic fallback to compatible variants during capacity constraints. Hyperscalers rarely provide same rollout granularity per-model.
- Deployment modes: Hosted API for speed, Dedicated for committed throughput, Private (VPC/on-prem) for regulated customers. Many APIs offer hosted only or require heavy custom infra for private deployments.
- Observability: Token-level tracing, per-query cost/latency, and eval-linked regression alerts. Competitors often give aggregate metrics only.
- Model catalog + verification: Curated open models with performance profiles and recommended quantization/ops. Many vendors provide models but not verified runtime profiles.

Common traps to avoid (what competitors bait on)
- "We can just switch later" — customers underestimate migration complexity: prompt drift, kv-cache behavior, and rollout dependencies make swaps non-trivial.
- Pricing headline: "cheaper per-token" — vendors quote aggressive per-token rates that ignore engineering and ops costs, fallback penalties, and long-tail latency effects.
- Feature parity only: Don’t get dragged into play-by-play feature lists if the buyer cares about operating guarantees and unit economics at scale.

Objection handling (short scripts)
1) "We already use CloudProviderAPI":
   - Empathy: "Totally reasonable — it's the easiest on-ramp."
   - Pivot: "If you start seeing latency spikes or sudden cost increases, Redwood can be slotted in with minimal code changes but give you better visibility, predictable cost levers (batching/cache), and controlled rollouts. We often step in once teams move from prototype to product."
2) "We can self-host to save money":
   - Empathy: "Self-hosting gives control but it adds months of infra work."
   - Pivot: "Redwood gives the same control (private & on-prem option), but with a lot of operational primitives pre-built — KV caching, autoscaling policies, and kernel selection — so you pay for shorter time-to-production and predictable ops overhead."
3) "Vendor X has cheaper token rates":
   - Empathy: "Price is important."
   - Pivot: "Total unit economics are more than token price. Ask about real-world SLOs, burst discounts, cache hit assumptions, and engineering time required to reach that published rate. We can run a short pilot to show delta on cost per useful-response, not just token consumption."
4) "We worry about model fidelity after quantization":
   - Answer: "We provide model-specific quantization profiles and run evals on your prompt sets to measure quality regressions. Optimize ties recommended profiles to rollout policies so you can test in canary buckets first."

Use-case-based quick scripts (for reps)
- Customer: "We need high-concurrency embeddings for search":
  Script: "Great — we have dedicated pools tuned for embeddings with predictable throughput and autoscaling. We also recommend batching and prefix caching; on pilot we can baseline your current qps and show the delta in latency and cost."
- Customer: "We have strict audit/KMS needs":
  Script: "Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit logs across the control plane. We can scope a VPC/on-prem plan and review required compliance documents—most enterprise customers appreciate the predictable security controls."

Competitive traps & guardrails for reps
- Don’t overpromise custom integrations or engineering velocity beyond the templated connectors we support (Slack, GCP, AWS, Datadog). Flag ??? for SE follow-up.
- Avoid claiming parity with every hyper-scale feature: instead, emphasize outcomes (SLA, unit economics, rollout safety).
- If a prospect uses model-specific features (e.g., proprietary embeddings), escalate to Solutions Engineering early.

Win themes by customer segment
- Startups (fast iteration): "Low friction hosted API + measurable cost tools so you can scale without sudden bills."
- Platform teams/enterprises: "Consistent inference contract across hosted/dedicated/private with SLOs, auditability, and rollout controls."
- Regulated orgs: "Private deployment paths, KMS integrations, and audit trails with a migration playbook."

Measurement hooks (to propose in pilots)
- Baseline token cost, response latency p90/p99, and failure/retry rate for 24–72h.
- Measure cost per successful end-to-end feature completion (e.g., helpful completion for chat flow, or search recall with embeddings).
- Quality check: run a small eval on customer prompts to measure changes in MRR/engagement signals (where applicable).

Open questions & risks to capture in deal notes
- Does the customer have hard SLOs for p99 latency or only soft targets?
- Are there existing caching/edge layers that would conflict with Redwood batching strategies?
- Data residency or contractual language around export controls/regulatory needs?

Quick-reference objection cheat-sheet (single-line responses)
- "We’re happy with CloudProviderAPI" -> "We integrate alongside them and show cost/latency deltas; minimal code changes for canary swap."
- "We’ll self-host" -> "We help with private deployment and reduce ops risk while preserving control."
- "Token rate is lower elsewhere" -> "We measure end-to-end cost on your workload, not list price; pilot shows the truth."

Tactical next steps for GTM teams (owners assigned)
- Sales enablement: record 10–15 minute roleplay videos of these scripts (Owner: Marco)
- SE playbook: expand technical checklist for private/DED migrations (Owner: Tomislav)
- Pilot template: create a 7–14 day pilot template that captures measurement hooks above (Owner: Lena)
- Update battlecard living doc weekly with new competitor price/feature moves (Owner: Aisha)

Notes and sources
- Pulled from internal trial decks, recent deal debriefs, and support tickets (anonymized).
- Add any competitor claim that materially affects a live deal to JIRA-PLAT-834 so we can update messaging centrally.

Short-term edits to make after next deal: 1) add competitor X's new fallback feature notes; 2) include SE migration checklist link.

End — keep this doc lightweight. The goal is quick recall on calls, not an exhaustive product manual. Update weekly as price moves and feature launches happen.
